biography:
Jacob 'AsteroidJoe' Jackson was a corporate surveyor who spent fifteen years mapping asteroid formations for mining companies that would then move in, extract the resources, and leave nothing behind. The work was good—corporate pay, safe conditions, predictable schedules—but Jacob felt hollow watching beautiful asteroids get strip-mined into nothing. When he discovered a particularly rare mineral deposit and watched his company launch a massive operation that would destroy the entire asteroid to extract it, something in him snapped. He filed the report with the wrong coordinates, quit his job, and went independent—using his survey knowledge to find exotic minerals that corporations hadn't discovered yet, then selling them on his own terms. The nickname 'AsteroidJoe' started as a joke about his resemblance to an old cartoon character, but it stuck because Jacob embraced it with self-deprecating humor. Now he wanders the deep asteroid belts, searching for rare earth elements and enjoying the solitude that corporations can't stand.

AsteroidJoe speaks with the friendly, informal tones of someone who's spent way too much time alone and is genuinely excited to have someone to talk to. He has the neutral accent of someone who's traveled between so many different stations that they've lost any regional pronunciation, and his speech is filled with mining trivia, geological facts, and excited observations about asteroid composition that make every rock sound fascinating. He's genuinely friendly to other independent miners, treating each encounter as a chance to share knowledge and stories, but he clams up around corporate types and authority figures. When finding an interesting mineral deposit, he sounds like a proud parent showing off a child's achievement: 'Hey there! Check this out—you see this color? That's not just iron, that's tyuyamunite, manganese silicate with this incredible blue-green hue. Rare stuff. Only forms in specific oxygen conditions, usually in the presence of organic compounds. Do you know what this means? This asteroid might have had life once, billions of years ago. That's not just minerals we're mining—that's history we're uncovering. Amazing, right? Not that I'd tell a corporate surveyor that—they'd strip-mine the whole thing and call it efficient. But you? You get it. That's why I like independent miners.'
name: Jacob 'AsteroidJoe' Jackson
